current_example.title: Example: Applying the Factor Theorem to Factors With Leading Coefficients

q-112455.name: Question 1
q-112455.problem:
For which of the following polynomials is $(x-2)$ a factor?

I. $f(x)={x}^{2}+3x-10$

II. $g(x)={x}^{3}+8$

III. $h(x)={x}^{3}+4x-16$
q-112455.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x-2).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =0 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

According to the factor theorem, $(x-2)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if the root $x=2$ is a root of $p(x).$ 

So now, we will check if $x=2$ is a root of the polynomials $f,$ $g$ and $h.$

- Evaluating $x=2$ at $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & ={2}^{2}+3(2)-10 \\  & =4+6-10 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(x-2)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$

- Now, evaluating $x=2$ at $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(2) & ={2}^{3}+8 \\  & =8+8 \\  & =16\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by the factor theorem, $(x-2)$ is not a factor of $g(x).$

- Finally, evaluating $x=2$ at $h(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}h(2) & ={2}^{3}+4(2)-16 \\  & =8+8-16 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(x-2)$ is indeed a factor of $h(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

So now, we will check if x=2 is a root of the polynomials f, g and h.

q-73772.name: Question 2
q-73772.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{2}+2x-3?$

I. $x=-3$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(x+3)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder
q-73772.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x+3).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+3 & =0 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

We now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $x=-3$ is a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3) & =(-3)^{2}+2(-3)-3 \\  & =9-6-3 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. According to the factor theorem, since $x=-3$ is a root of $f(x),$ then $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is true. If $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ then $(x+3)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

q-112486.name: Question 3
q-112486.problem:
For which of the following polynomials is $(5x+4)$ a factor?

I. $f(x)=5{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}$

II. $g(x)=15{x}^{2}+25x+4$

III. $h(x)=4{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}$
q-112486.worked_solution:
According to the factor theorem, $(ax-b)$ is a factor of the polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=\frac{b}{a}$ is also root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(5x+4).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+4 & =0 \\ 5x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

According to the factor theorem, then, $(5x+4)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ is a root of $p(x).$

Now we will check if $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ is a root of the polynomials $f,$ $g$ and $h.$

- Evaluating $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ at $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-\frac{4}{5}) & =5{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{3}+4{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =5(-\frac{64}{125})+4(\frac{16}{25}) \\  & =-\frac{64}{25}+\frac{64}{25} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(5x+4)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$

- Now, evaluating $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ at $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-\frac{4}{5}) & =15{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2}+25(-\frac{4}{5})+4 \\  & =15(\frac{16}{25})-20+4 \\  & =\frac{48}{5}-16 \\  & =-\frac{32}{5}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by the factor theorem, $(5x+4)$ is not a factor of $g(x).$

- Finally, evaluating $x=-\frac{4}{5}$ at $h(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-\frac{4}{5}) & =4{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{3}+5{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =4(-\frac{64}{125})+5(\frac{16}{25}) \\  & =-\frac{256}{125}+\frac{16}{5} \\  & =\frac{144}{125}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by the factor theorem, $(5x+4)$ is not a factor of $g(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Here, we are considering (5x+4). The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to 0 and solving:

5x+4=05x=−4x=−45

According to the factor theorem, then, (5x+4) is a factor of p(x) if x=−45 is a root of p(x).

Now we will check if x=−45 is a root of the polynomials f, g and h.

  • Evaluating x=−45 at f(x), we get f(−45)=5(−45)3+4(−45)2=5(−64125)+4(1625)=−6425+6425=0. Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that (5x+4) is indeed a factor of f(x).
  • Now, evaluating x=−45 at g(x), we get g(−45)=15(−45)2+25(−45)+4=15(1625)−20+4=485−16=−325≠0. So, by the factor theorem, (5x+4) is not a factor of g(x).
  • Finally, evaluating x=−45 at h(x), we get h(−45)=4(−45)3+5(−45)2=4(−64125)+5(1625)=−256125+165=144125≠0. So, by the factor theorem, (5x+4) is not a factor of g(x).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

q-112465.name: Question 4
q-112465.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)=4{x}^{2}-25?$

I. $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(2x-5)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(2x-5)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder
q-112465.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(ax-b)$ is a factor of the polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=\frac{b}{a}$ is also root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(2x-5).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-5 & =0 \\ 2x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{5}{2}) & =4{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-25 \\  & =4(\frac{25}{4})-25 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. According to the factor theorem, since $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is a root of $f(x),$ then $(2x-5)$ is a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is true. Since $(2x-5)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ then $(2x-5)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
